In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel notion of privacy, label differential privacy (LDP), which requires that the trained model is insensitive to small changes in the labels of the examples.
a privacy notion that has received little attention in the literature, but that is important for several practical applications.

The paper proposes two new approaches to label differential privacy (LDP) that can be used in conjunction with the PATE framework for training a model.
, for the problem of training a model on a dataset of labeled data, there is no single best approach to privacy, as different approaches have different trade-offs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the label DP problem can be solved by a combination of two techniques: (1) using the label as the private attribute, and (2) using the label to train the model.
we show that DP can be achieved on labels without sacrificing the utility of the learned model, and in many cases, we can even achieve a better utility compared to the standard approach.
the Laplace mechanism can be used to train differentially private models, while the PATE framework is useful for training differentially private models with high accuracy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the label DP requirement does not necessarily imply that the model is trained on noisy labels: in fact, our proposed methods are able to train models that achieve state-of-the-art performance, while satisfying DP with respect to labels.
label privacy is not only feasible, but also can be achieved with much less noise than the standard setting of DP with respect to the entire dataset.
the label DP setting is fundamentally different from the data DP setting.
